                      fig.height = 5)

```{r setup}
library(imisr)
```

## What IMIS does

Incremental mixture importance sampling (IMIS) draws from a posterior
distribution $p(\theta \mid y) \propto p(\theta) L(\theta)$ and, at no extra
cost, estimates the marginal likelihood
$p(y) = \int p(\theta) L(\theta)\, d\theta$, which Bayes factors and Bayesian
model averaging need.

It starts from a large sample of the prior. Draws with large importance
weights sit in regions the current sampling function covers poorly, so IMIS
places a multivariate normal component on the highest-weight draw, samples
from it, and recomputes all weights against the enlarged mixture. It repeats
until the weights are close to uniform. Because the prior always stays in
the mixture, the weights are bounded and the estimates are unbiased (Raftery
and Bao, 2010).

The draws are independent, so there is no burn-in, no thinning and no
autocorrelation. The method is well suited to posteriors that are
concentrated on thin ridges or have several modes, which are typical when
calibrating mechanistic and simulation models.

## The three functions you write

`imis()` needs:

| Argument | What it does | Returns |
|---|---|---|
| `sample_prior(n)` | draws `n` parameter sets from the prior | `n` x `d` matrix with column names |
| `log_prior(theta)` | log prior density (normalized) | one value per parameter set |
| `log_likelihood(theta)` | log-likelihood | one value per parameter set |

By default, `log_prior()` and `log_likelihood()` receive a matrix with one
parameter set per row. Set `vectorized = FALSE` to write them for a single
named parameter vector instead, which is usually more natural for simulation
models (see `vignette("calibrating-simulation-models")`).

Everything is on the **log scale**. A log-likelihood of $-2400$ is
unremarkable when calibrating to many targets, but $e^{-2400}$ is zero in
double precision, which is why the original 'IMIS' package could fail on
such problems.

## A first example with a known answer

Four observations $y_i \sim N(\mu, 1)$ with prior $\mu \sim N(0, 2^2)$. The
posterior and the marginal likelihood are available in closed form, so we
can check the answer.

```{r conjugate}
y <- c(1.2, 0.8, 1.9, 1.4)

log_likelihood <- function(theta) {
  # y_i - mu, with one column per parameter set
  colSums(dnorm(outer(y, theta[, "mu"], "-"), log = TRUE))
}
log_prior <- function(theta) dnorm(theta[, "mu"], 0, 2, log = TRUE)
sample_prior <- function(n) cbind(mu = rnorm(n, 0, 2))

set.seed(1)
fit <- imis(log_likelihood, log_prior, sample_prior, verbose = FALSE)
fit
```

The exact values:

```{r conjugate-exact}
post_prec <- length(y) + 1 / 4
c(mean = sum(y) / post_prec, sd = sqrt(1 / post_prec))
s_y <- diag(length(y)) + 4
c(log_ml = -0.5 * (length(y) * log(2 * pi) +
                     determinant(s_y)$modulus[1] +
                     drop(y %*% solve(s_y, y))))
```

`summary()` uses all IMIS draws with their importance weights. The
equally weighted resample, for downstream simulation, is in `fit$resample`
(or `as.matrix(fit)`).

```{r resample}
head(as.matrix(fit))
```

### Diagnostics

`plot(fit)` shows how the estimates evolved over the stages. The marginal
likelihood estimate should settle down, the effective sample size (ESS) should
grow, and IMIS stops once the expected number of unique points in the
resample reaches the dashed line, $1 - e^{-1} \approx 63\%$ of the resample
size. That is the value expected if the sampling function were exactly the
posterior.

```{r diagnostics}
plot(fit)
```

The same numbers are in `fit$diagnostics`.

## Several modes: IMIS-opt and several components per iteration

IMIS can only refine regions where the prior sample landed. When the
posterior has several modes that the prior sample may have missed, use an
*optimization stage* (`n_optim`). It runs that many local optimizations from
high-weight draws and starts the mixture with a normal component at each
mode. Alternatively, adding several components per iteration
(`n_centers`) spreads the new components across separate high-weight
regions.

The bimodal example from Raftery and Bao (2010) has two narrow, oppositely
correlated modes:

```{r bimodal}
ar_chol <- function(r) chol(matrix(c(1, r, r, 1), 2))
log_lik_bimodal <- function(theta) {
  l1 <- mvn_log(theta, c(0, 0), ar_chol(-0.95))
  l2 <- mvn_log(theta, c(9, 9), ar_chol(0.95))
  log(0.5) + pmax(l1, l2) + log1p(exp(-abs(l1 - l2)))
}
mvn_log <- function(x, mu, r) {
  z <- backsolve(r, t(x) - mu, transpose = TRUE)
  -0.5 * colSums(z^2) - sum(log(diag(r))) - log(2 * pi)
}
log_prior_box <- function(theta) rowSums(dunif(theta, -3, 12, log = TRUE))
sample_box <- function(n) {
  matrix(runif(2 * n, -3, 12), n, 2, dimnames = list(NULL, c("a", "b")))
}

set.seed(2)
fit_opt <- imis(log_lik_bimodal, log_prior_box, sample_box, n_optim = 5,
                verbose = FALSE)
fit_opt
```

Half of the resample should be in each mode, and the exact log marginal
likelihood is $-2\log 15 \approx -5.416$:

```{r bimodal-check}
mean(fit_opt$resample[, "a"] > 4.5)
```

```{r bimodal-plot, fig.height = 6}
plot(fit_opt, type = "pairs")
```

Red stars are the mixture component centers.

## Which settings to change

| Situation | Setting |
|---|---|
| Model runs are slow | `parallel = TRUE` (see below) |
| Posterior may be multimodal, or far from the prior | `n_optim = 10` |
| Several separated high-probability regions | `n_centers > 1` and/or `sampling = "mixture"` |
| Stopping too early or too late | `target_unique`, `max_iter` |
| Each new component should be estimated from more draws | `n_per_component` |
| Some parameter combinations make the model invalid | `catch_errors = TRUE` |
| Likelihood written for one parameter vector | `vectorized = FALSE` |

`sampling = "incremental"` (the default, as in Raftery and Bao, 2010) takes
new draws only from the newest components. `sampling = "mixture"` (as in
Steele, Raftery and Emond, 2006) draws from the whole current mixture,
including a share `prior_weight` from the prior, so earlier components keep
getting draws. Either way every draw is weighted against the full mixture,
so both are unbiased.

## Parallel computing

When one model run takes milliseconds or more, evaluating the likelihood is
the bottleneck. With `parallel = TRUE`, `imis()` splits each batch of draws
into blocks evaluated in parallel through the
[future](https://future.futureverse.org) framework. You choose where they
run:

```{r parallel, eval = FALSE}
library(future)
plan(multisession, workers = 4) # or multicore, cluster, future.batchtools...
fit <- imis(log_likelihood, log_prior, sample_prior, parallel = TRUE)
plan(sequential)
```

Results are reproducible with `set.seed()`. For fast models like the ones in
this vignette, sending work to other R processes costs more than it saves.
Time a serial run first.

## Comparing models

The marginal likelihoods of two models fitted to the same data give their
Bayes factor, with a Monte Carlo standard error:

```{r bf}
set.seed(3)
fit_shifted <- imis(log_likelihood,
                    function(theta) dnorm(theta[, "mu"], 3, 1, log = TRUE),
                    function(n) cbind(mu = rnorm(n, 3, 1)), verbose = FALSE)
bayes_factor(fit, fit_shifted)
```

## Coming from the 'IMIS' package

`imis_legacy()` accepts the arguments of the archived `IMIS::IMIS()` and
finds `prior()`, `likelihood()` and `sample.prior()` in the calling
environment, as `IMIS()` did. Old scripts run unchanged:

```{r legacy, eval = FALSE}
result <- imis_legacy(B = 1000, B.re = 3000, number_k = 100, D = 0)
result$resample
```

To move to `imis()`:

| `IMIS()` | `imis()` |
|---|---|
| `likelihood(x)` (natural scale) | `log_likelihood` (log scale) |
| `prior(x)` | `log_prior` |
| `sample.prior(n)` | `sample_prior` |
| `B` | `n_per_component` |
| `B * 10` (fixed) | `n_initial` |
| `B.re` | `n_resample` |
| `number_k` | `max_iter + 1` |
| `D` | `n_optim` |
| `$stat`, `$center` | `$diagnostics`, `$centers` |

## References

Raftery AE, Bao L (2010). Estimating and projecting trends in HIV/AIDS
generalized epidemics using incremental mixture importance sampling.
*Biometrics*, 66(4), 1162-1173.

Steele RJ, Raftery AE, Emond MJ (2006). Computing normalizing constants for
finite mixture models via incremental mixture importance sampling (IMIS).
*Journal of Computational and Graphical Statistics*, 15(3), 712-734.
